paper_metadata.title: Quantum unary approach to option pricing

summary: The paper presents a gate-based unary quantum algorithm for European option pricing under the Black-Scholes model, using amplitude distribution loading, controlled-Ry payoff encoding, and iterative amplitude estimation without QPE. The main numerical study uses 8 unary qubits versus 3 binary qubits, with noisy Qiskit simulations under up to 0.5% single-qubit error, 1% two-qubit error, and 5% readout error; the authors report better robustness for the unary circuit, but no practical quantum advantage over classical pricing is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Gate-based unary quantum algorithm for European option pricing using amplitude distribution loading, payoff encoding, and iterative amplitude estimation; evaluated via classical simulation on 8-qubit unary and 3-qubit binary instances under ideal and noisy conditions.

algorithm.variant: Unary option pricing with iterative amplitude estimation (no QPE)
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterative AE with repeated measurements; confidence interval based selection of the most probable angle/value

hyperparameters.m_j_sequence: linear mj=j and exponential mj={0}∪{2^j} discussed in appendix
hyperparameters.alpha: 0.05 for main iterative AE analysis; appendix also analyzes alpha=3/4 (linear) and alpha=1 (exponential) bounds
hyperparameters.Nshots: 10000 in several simulations; 104 samples per experiment for distribution loading and payoff/noise studies
hyperparameters.num_bins: 8 bins for main AE comparisons; scalability shown up to 20 bins

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial unary state prepared by applying a single X gate to the middle qubit; AE starts with m0=0

optimizer_settings.notes: No classical optimizer; iterative AE uses weighted averaging of measured angles

classical_baselines: Classical Monte Carlo / classical expected payoff computation
Binary quantum option-pricing algorithm from prior work used as comparison baseline

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Unary basis: one qubit in |1> identifies the asset-price bin; 8 unary qubits correspond to 8 bins in the main comparison. Payoff is encoded by controlled Ry rotations on an ancilla for bins above strike.
problem_formulation.objective_function: European call payoff C = E[max(0, S_T - K)] under Black-Scholes log-normal distribution; ancilla probability encodes normalized expected payoff
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Post-selection on unary subspace; discard outcomes not having exactly one |1> in the register

problem_instance.description: European option pricing under Black-Scholes model for a single asset; main numerical example uses S0=2, sigma=40%, r=5%, T=0.1 years, K=1.9

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic log-normal asset-price distribution at maturity; discretized into bins

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical computation of target log-normal probabilities; binning over approximately three standard deviations from the mean; exact classical payoff used as reference with 10^4 bins
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 100 repetitions for many experiments; 10 repetitions for larger-bin scalability study; comparisons made against classical exact/Monte Carlo values and against binary quantum baseline

noise_model.noise_type: depolarizing noise plus symmetric measurement/readout error

implementation_details.transpilation_target: ideal chip structures with nearest-neighbor interactions and ancilla connectivity; no explicit transpilation settings reported
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Compute Black-Scholes probabilities and angles for partial-SWAP gates; discretize distribution into bins; derive payoff rotation angles
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Weighted-average iterative AE post-processing; convert ancilla probability to payoff by multiplying by normalization factor; discard non-unary measurement outcomes

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: AE convergence shown over M=0..4 iterations; payoff uncertainty decreases with iterations

speedup_claims.conditions: Amplitude Estimation with sufficiently accurate state preparation; idealized quantum setting
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes this is only achievable when the probability distribution of the asset price can be loaded efficiently; NISQ noise and state-preparation overhead can reduce practical advantage.

speedup_claims.factor: better than binary for fewer than ~100 bins/qubits in NISQ regime
speedup_claims.conditions: Near-term noisy devices, ideal chip connectivity assumptions in gate-count comparison
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a practical crossover claim from gate-count/noise simulations, not an asymptotic advantage; binary may outperform unary at larger bin counts if hardware were ideal.

speedup_claims.conditions: Iterative AE without QPE; depends on the chosen mj schedule (linear or exponential)
speedup_claims.caveats: These are uncertainty scalings, not wall-clock speedups; they assume the iterative AE post-processing model described in the appendix.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Amplitude estimation gives quadratic improvement in number of circuit calls; unary circuit depth O(n) for distribution and O(kappa n) for payoff; iterative AE without QPE discussed as O(Nshots^-1/2 M^-1) or O(Nshots^-1/2 M^-3/4) depending on mj schedule
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo sampling scales as O(N^-1/2) in estimation error; exact classical binning/payoff computation used as reference
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Paper suggests unary may be advantageous for fewer than ~100 bins/qubits in NISQ regime; gate-count crossover around <100 bins

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Paper suggests a crossover around <100 bins/qubits for gate count, but this is only a structural estimate, not a demonstrated runtime advantage.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 8 unary qubits for the main noisy-simulation comparison; 3 binary qubits for the baseline; 100 repetitions in many plots; 10^4 samples for some studies; iterative AE with M=0..4.
limiting_factors: Classical preprocessing for distribution loading and angle synthesis remains required
Binary baseline is only a comparison target, not a classical competitor

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_noisy because the paper states simulations were carried out with Qiskit and models depolarizing/readout noise, with no real QPU named.

circuit_depth not given as a single numeric value for the full experiment; only asymptotic/structural depths are reported (e.g., distributor depth floor(n/2)+1, gate-count table, and AE iteration structure).
The paper argues the unary circuit is shallower and more noise-robust than the binary quantum baseline, but it does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical methods.
Reported results are noisy simulations only; the classical Monte Carlo baseline remains the reference for correctness.
